n: Rehoboam goes north to Shechem to be confirmed as king. That he must travel there shows the northern tribes expected to negotiate, not simply accept him.

f.g: an ancient city in the hill country of Ephraim, where Joshua renewed the covenant.

n: News of the gathering reaches Jeroboam, who had been in exile in Egypt since fleeing Solomon.

f.w: was fled from the presence of king Solomon

n: The northern tribes call Jeroboam home, and he becomes their spokesman before Rehoboam.
Their request is reasonable: Solomon’s taxes and forced labor were crushing. Lighten the load, and they will gladly serve.

f.g: the wooden bar on an ox’s neck; a symbol of burdens and servitude.
heavy, burdensome.

n: Rehoboam asks for three days to consider his answer.
He first asks the elder statesmen who had advised Solomon.

f.g: served as officials of; attended.

n: Their counsel is a timeless principle of leadership: serve the people and speak kindly to them today, and they will serve you for life. It echoes the Savior’s teaching that the greatest is the servant of all.

f.w: be a servant unto this people

n: Rehoboam rejects that advice and turns to the young men he grew up with, now his courtiers.

f.g: abandoned, rejected.

n: He asks them how to answer the people’s request.
Their advice is to be harsh. “My little finger is thicker than my father’s loins” is a crude boast: “My smallest effort will outweigh my father’s greatest.”

f.g: waist or hips.

n: They suggest he promise heavier burdens. “Scorpions” may refer to a barbed or weighted whip—punishment far worse than before.

f.g: load, burden.
probably a whip tipped with sharp points or weights.

n: On the third day Jeroboam and the people return as instructed.
Rehoboam speaks harshly, ignoring the experienced counselors.

f.g: harshly, severely.

n: He repeats the young men’s threats almost word for word. It is a fatal miscalculation.
The narrator sees God’s hand at work: Rehoboam’s pride became the means by which Ahijah’s prophecy was fulfilled. God allows human choices to accomplish His purposes.

f.w: the cause was from the LORD

n: The northern tribes revolt with a rallying cry: “What share do we have in David?” “To your tents” meant “Go home—we’re done.” The same cry had been raised in an earlier rebellion under Sheba.

f.w: see to thine own house, David
f.g: look after your own family; Israel no longer belongs to you.

n: Rehoboam keeps only the Israelites living in Judah.
Rehoboam foolishly sends Adoram, the very official in charge of forced labor, to restore order. The people stone him, and the king flees in his chariot.

f.g: also called Adoniram, overseer of forced labor.
here, forced labor.

n: The split becomes permanent. From now on “Israel” usually means the northern kingdom and “Judah” the southern.
Israel’s assembly crowns Jeroboam. Only Judah remains loyal to David’s house, just as prophesied.
Rehoboam gathers a huge army of 180,000 from Judah and Benjamin to win back the north by force.

f.g: the small tribe north of Jerusalem that sided with Judah.
eighty.

n: The Lord intervenes through Shemaiah, a prophet in Judah.
The message goes to the king and all the people of Judah and Benjamin.
The Lord forbids civil war: these are their brothers, and the division is His doing. To their credit, Rehoboam and the people obey and go home.

f.g: God claims the division as His judgment, not mere politics.

n: Jeroboam fortifies Shechem as his capital, then Penuel east of the Jordan.

f.g: a town east of the Jordan where Jacob wrestled.

n: Here the turn begins. Jeroboam reasons privately, not with the Lord, and fears losing his kingdom—despite God’s promise to him.
His fear is political: if his people keep worshiping at Jerusalem’s temple, their loyalty may drift back to Rehoboam, and they may kill him.

Jeroboam makes two golden calves and presents them with Aaron’s very words at Sinai. Whether meant as idols or as pedestals for an invisible God, they broke the commandment and imitated Israel’s first great apostasy.

f.g: young bulls; bull imagery was common in Canaanite worship.

n: He places one at Bethel in the south of his kingdom and one at Dan in the far north—convenient alternatives to Jerusalem.

f.g: ‘house of God,’ where Jacob saw his ladder.

n: It became a national sin. People traveled as far as Dan to worship. This “sin of Jeroboam” becomes the standard by which every later northern king is judged.
He also built shrines on high places and appointed priests from any background, not from the tribe of Levi as the law required. Many Levites then left for Judah.

f.g: better, ‘from all sorts of people’—anyone, not just Levites.

n: Jeroboam created a rival feast one month after Judah’s Feast of Tabernacles, and personally offered sacrifices to the calves at Bethel.

f.w: the feast that is in Judah
f.g: the Feast of Tabernacles, held on the 15th day of the seventh month.

n: The narrator stresses that the date was “devised of his own heart.” Jeroboam’s religion was man-made, designed to serve his political needs rather than God’s commands.

f.g: invented by himself, not commanded by God.
